21089-young-tom-bowling-the-boys-of-the-:
J. C. Hutcheson wrote this novel about how boy seamen were trained in the Royal Navy at the end of the nineteenth century. Tom trains for just over a year aboard Saint Vincent before moving on to postings in the fleet. Boys from many parts of Britain serve with him, each with his own dialect.

One shipmate, nicknamed Ugly, meets a sad and noble end. Later service takes Tom to the East African coast, where British ships hunted and punished slave traders. Hutcheson follows drills, signals, and daily routine closely. The book preserves the feel of a training ship from inside.
24030-stories-from-livy:
The Reverend Alfred Church, professor of Latin in University College, London, published Stories from Livy with Scribner and Welford in 1883, with illustrations from designs by Pinelli. His preface explains that a stroke of illness kept him from correcting the proofs, a work carried out for him by his friend C. Simmons of Balliol College, Oxford.

Church wished to say a few words on the difficulty of turning Livy's elaborate language into the plain style he favored. The stories begin with Romulus and Numa: Aeneas of Troy takes Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus, to wife, and builds Lavinium. His son Ascanius builds Alba, where kings of Aeneas's line reign for twelve generations. Procas leaves his kingdom to Numitor the elder, but Amulius drives out his brother, slays his brother's sons, and makes Rhea Silvia a priestess of Vesta.
24615-a-middy-of-the-king-a-romance-of-t:
Harry Collingwood wrote this romance of the old British Navy, following Dick Delamere, a midshipman on leave recalled to join the Europa at Portsmouth. The action falls in the very late eighteenth century, when Britain stood hostile to France and Holland. Early chapters patrol the Channel and the Bay of Biscay.

Later the Europa sails to the West Indies, where pirates infest the waters and must be rooted out. Collingwood describes naval life, engagements, and shipboard routine with care. Young readers get a stirring sea tale of a middy learning his trade, in the age of sail and cannon.
25764-reminiscences-of-two-years-in-the-:
John M. Batten, late acting assistant surgeon in the United States Navy, writes these reminiscences of two years in the navy, printed for the author in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in 1881. Batten, writing from Pittsburgh, excuses the little book by saying a story half told beats a story not told at all.

He dedicates the book to the Grand Army of the Republic, to soldiers and sailors who gave lives for the Union, and to his mother Sarah Batten. As a navy surgeon, Batten saw service, sickness, and shipboard life during the Civil War era, and his short memoir preserves a medical officer's plain, personal view.
32437-the-automobile-girls-at-chicago-or:
Laura Dent Crane's girls' novel, copyrighted in 1912, sends the Automobile Girls to Chicago, where they must win out against heavy odds. Early chapters bring a man in section thirteen, a missing passenger, a dizzy round of pleasure, and a battle of bulls and bears. A wreck, a mystery of iron gates, a secret passage, and an Indian graveyard follow, with a treasure hunter and a curious old journal.

Later the girls give an attic party, solve the mystery of the attic, and watch Tommy take a wild ride. Crane, author of the Automobile Girls at Newport, in the Berkshires, and along the Hudson, mixes motoring, city life, and mystery. Young readers get adventure, friendship, and pluck, with Chicago's streets, hotels, and stock-exchange talk as a lively backdrop.
342-margaret-ogilvy:
J. M. Barrie remembers his mother through six hair-bottomed chairs bought on the day he was born. Margaret Ogilvy, in its 1897 second edition, opens with that purchase: a pound-note and thirty threepenny bits, a white-faced father, and a west room triumph. Barrie heard the tale so often it feels like memory.

Later chapters follow his mother's soft face, her reading, and her grief for a lost son. Barrie writes a son's love letter to a Scottish mother. The book, dedicated to his sister Jane Ann, moves without sentimentality. It shows the roots of Peter Pan's creator.
4076-the-discovery-of-muscovy:
A volume from Richard Hakluyt's collections tells how England first reached Muscovy, now Russia, in Queen Elizabeth's reign. The voyages of Ohthere and Wulfstan from King Alfred's Orosius join the main account, giving the book a long view of northern seas.

Chapters describe Russian bondage, where men sell wives and children for ready money and content themselves with meat and drink. A law of mercy beats thieves rather than hanging them at first. Readers who like early travel writing will find a vivid record of first contact between England and Russia.
britannica-1911-basil-muscovy:
Basil, in Russian Vasily, is the shared name of four grand dukes and tsars of Muscovy treated together in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Basil I Dmitrevich (1371–1425) made the grand duchy practically hereditary, annexed Suzdal and other places, yet still paid tribute to the Golden Horde. Basil II, called the Blind (1415–1462), survived seizure, blinding, and banishment while Moscow steadily absorbed district after district around him.

Later rulers complete the set. Basil III Ivanovich (1479–1533) annexed the last independent principalities, took Pskov's charter away in 1510, and captured Smolensk from Poland with artillery supplied through Michael Glinsky. Basil IV, Shuisky (died 1612), rose by betraying both sides in the Demetrius affair. He reigned from 1606 without ever being generally recognized, and was deposed in 1610 and carried off to Warsaw. Taken together, the four lives trace Moscow's climb from tribute-paying duchy to tsardom.
britannica-1911-cavy:
The text hosted under this record is not an article on the cavy. It is the closing portion of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography of Cavour, the Italian statesman, and it opens in mid argument. In the portion hosted here, Cavour holds to his principle of a free church in a free state. His dream of a free and united Italy stands realised, save for Rome and Venice. The strain of the last years, above all the talks with Garibaldi, wears him down.

The hosted text follows the end closely. A painful scene with Garibaldi in the chamber over Nice hastens his decline. Fever follows a short illness, and he dies on 6 June 1861. He is buried at his ancestral castle of Santena. The closing judgment calls him the greatest figure of the Risorgimento. His secretary Artom is quoted on the deep sense of reality that set Cavour apart from dreamers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-donlev:
Little is known about Andrew Donlevy's early life. This educator was born in 1694, probably in Sligo, Ireland, and his date and place of death are uncertain. Penal laws were then enforced with rigour, so getting an education at home was hard; going abroad for the priesthood was a crime, so he must have travelled in disguise. He reached Paris in 1710 and joined the Irish College as a student.

Once his clerical course was finished, he was ordained priest, and in 1728 he became prefect of the college, holding that office until 1746. He had also attended university lectures, graduating in both theology and law. As prefect, he drew up a new code of rules for running the college, putting it under the Archbishop of Paris and subject to the university. In 1742 he brought out an Irish-English catechism of Christian Doctrine; Dublin saw another edition in 1848.
margaret-ogilvy:
Margaret Ogilvy is J. M. Barrie's portrait of his mother, written by her son. This second edition of 1897 completed its twentieth thousand. Barrie dedicated it to the memory of his sister Jane Ann. Its first chapter asks how his mother got her soft face.

He begins with six hair-bottomed chairs bought the day he was born. That purchase was the first great victory of her long campaign. Poverty, thrift, and triumph fill her Scots household in his telling. Barrie writes in her own dialect, with love in every line. The creator of Peter Pan here explains his truest source. Margaret Ogilvy remains one of literature's tenderest mother books.
podcast-dannyjones-d6DTpoaxevY:
Sean Stone joins Danny Jones to claim that a secret society, not the Freemasons alone, truly runs the world. The episode title frames him as an ex-Freemason with a reveal. Stone is a filmmaker and the son of Oliver Stone.

Stone tells what he says he learned inside lodges and in his work since. He argues a smaller, richer group sits above the groups most people name. Jones asks how Stone knows and what proof he can show. Listeners get the claim whole, with the host testing each step. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-dannyjones-wqoIa7GQcvY:
Former CIA officer Andrew Bustamante joins Danny Jones and warns that America is about to fall. The episode title says a CIA super spy at last breaks cover. Bustamante now teaches spy skills to the public through his firm.

Bustamante lays out the rot he sees in US power, from debt to weak will. He uses his spy past to read foes and friends alike. Jones asks what a fall would look like and who would rise. Listeners get a stark warning from a trained eye. The library holds the talk as an archive record of his stated view.
the-discovery-of-muscovy:
The Discovery of Muscovy, printed by Cassell and Company in 1893 for Cassell's National Library. It is drawn from the collections of Richard Hakluyt, with the voyages of Ohthere and Wulfstan from King Alfred's Orosius added. An introduction explains that England's first relations with Russia were set up in Queen Elizabeth's reign by the expedition of Sir Hugh Willoughby, completed by Richard Chancellor, captain of the Edward Bonaventure.

Chancellor sailed on after a North Sea storm parted the ships; Willoughby and his crews were frozen to death. The tale of Chancellor's voyage and the bids to open Muscovy to English trade is given as Hakluyt told it in his folio of 1589. The first contact, the introduction adds, belongs to the days of Ivan the Terrible.
the-story-of-ivy:
Marie Belloc Lowndes published this novel in 1927, presented here in a Saga Egmont ebook edition of 2022 that republishes it as a historical document. The prologue opens at a country-house weekend party. Lady Flora Desmond asks her hostess about the Lextons. The hostess is Mary Hampton. Lady Flora remarks on Ivy Lexton's face. She has never seen a prettier one.

Mrs. Hampton admits, with some tartness, that the Lextons were invited so they could make friends with her millionaire guest, a fine amateur billiard player. Yet Miles Rushworth is not watching the billiards. The other men watch without him. He strolls in the moonlight across the lawn with Ivy. They head toward an avenue of beeches. The sharp-tongued Joan Rodney is on hand. She points out the contradiction.
